available in rooms, or gave condoms directly to couples, with and without the presence of health-education material
in the rooms. In a factorial design we assessed condom use directly by searching the rooms after couples had
left.Findings11 motels were used mainly by sex workers and their clients and eight mainly for non-commercial sex.
6463 couples attended the motels in 24 days. On 3106 (48·0%) occasions, at least one used condom was retrieved.
Condom use was more frequent for commercial sex than for non-commercial sex (60·5 vs 20·2%). The presence of
health-education material lowered the frequency of condom use for commercial sex (odds ratio 0·89 [95% CI
0·84–0·94\]) and had no effect on use for non-commercial sex (1·03 [0·97–1·08\]). Condom use increased for
commercial (1·31 [1·09–1·75\]) and noncommercial sex (1·81 (1·14–2·81) if condoms were available in rooms. Directly
handing condoms to couples was similarly effective for commercial sex but less effective for non-commercial sex
(1·32 [1·03–1·61\] vs 1·52 [1·01–2·38\]).InterpretationIn Latin America, motels are key locations for promoting the
use of condoms. Making condoms available in rooms is the most effective strategy to increase condom use, whereas use
of health-education material was ineffective. These findings have important implications for HIV-prevention

# Prepare narrative sections
short_version = """### 1. Task outcome (short version):
Extracted PICO, settings, study design, follow-up, and quantitative outcomes from 11 included studies of behavioral
interventions among sex workers/clients (and related high-risk settings) in LMICs. Key findings: counseling-enhanced
condom promotion modestly reduced aggregate STIs and increased condom use in Madagascar (ORs ~0.7 and 1.4); providing
the option of female condoms in Thailand reduced unprotected acts and STD incidence rates but not significantly; an
adapted VCT in China improved consistent condom use (OR 2.23) and reduced STDs (OR 0.44); a brief intervention in Mexico
reduced combined STI incidence density (P=0.034) and HIV incidence density (P<0.001); community-level interventions in
Uganda did not reduce HIV-1 incidence but improved some STI outcomes and condom use; motel-based structural
interventions in Nicaragua showed in-room condom availability increased use (ORs 1.31–1.81), while educational materials
were ineffective or harmful for commercial sex. Other RCTs (South Africa, Armenia, Zimbabwe, India) showed improvements
in risk behaviors and feasibility, with limited biomarker data in some."""

detailed_version = """### 2. Task outcome (extremely detailed version):
- Madagascar (Study 2, RCT, n=1000 FSWs): Peer+clinic counseling vs peer-only increased reported condom use (overall OR
1.4; 95% CI 1.1–1.8) and reduced aggregate STI prevalence (OR 0.7; 95% CI 0.5–0.9); specific STIs had ORs 0.7–0.8 with
CIs crossing/null for some. 6-month follow-up; STI biomarkers and self-reports; minimal confounding after adjustment.
- Thailand (Study 3, cluster RCT by establishment; 249 vs 255 FSWs): Option to use female condoms yielded high overall
condom use (≈98%), reduced unprotected acts (5.9% vs 7.1%; P=0.16) and STD incidence rates (2.81 vs 3.69/100 PY;
P=0.18), but not statistically significant. Female condom use sustained; design minimized cross-over.
- Madagascar (Study 6, RCT, n=901): Adding clinic-based counseling to peer education (male+female condom promotion)
showed no significant differences in aggregated STI prevalence or reported protection. 12-month follow-up; prior
intensive male condom promotion exposure.
- China Guangxi (Study 7, quasi-experimental, n=400 FSWs): Adapted VCT increased consistent condom use (OR 2.23; 95% CI
1.26–3.96) and reduced any STD infection at follow-up (OR 0.44; 95% CI 0.24–0.80); large gains in knowledge (p<.0001).
6-month follow-up; lab-confirmed STDs.
- Mexico (Study 8, RCT, n=924 FSWs): 30-min behavioral intervention reduced cumulative STI incidence (P=0.049); combined
STI incidence density 13.8 vs 24.92/100 PY (P=0.034) and HIV incidence density 0 vs 2.01/100 PY (P<0.001); protected
acts increased, unprotected acts decreased (P<0.05). 6-month follow-up; multiple biomarkers.
- South Africa (Study 10, RCT, n=93; 80 at 1-mo): Woman-Focused intervention decreased unprotected sex and daily
alcohol/cocaine use; greater substance-use reductions vs Standard; lower victimization reported. Short follow-up;
self-reports; feasibility shown.
- Armenia (Study 12, RCT, n=120 street-based FSWs): 2-hour, skills-based/gender-empowerment session increased consistent
condom use (P=0.004) and performing condom application (P=0.0001) over 6 months; psychosocial mediators improved.
- Zimbabwe (Study 14, RCT, n=149): Access to male+female vs male-only condoms increased consistent male condom use with
clients by 2 weeks (0→52% vs 0→82%); female condom use remained low (3–9%); STI incidence 16/100 woman-months; lower use
with boyfriends; high baseline HIV (86%) and 34% STI.
- India, Chennai (Study 15, RCT pilot, n=100): Microenterprise (canvas bag tailoring) associated with fewer paying
clients per month and increased income; fewer sex partners; sustained engagement in bag production; no biomarker data in
abstract.
- Uganda (Study 26, community cluster RCT, 18 communities): Behavioral (A) and behavioral+STI (B) vs control (C): No
HIV-1 incidence reduction (A vs C RR 0.94; 95% CI 0.60–1.45; p=0.72; B vs C RR 1.00; 0.63–1.58; p=0.98). Condom use with
last casual partner improved, significantly in B (PR 1.27; 1.02–1.56). HSV-2 incidence reduced in A (RR 0.65;
0.53–0.80); active syphilis (RR 0.52; 0.27–0.98) and gonorrhoea prevalence (RR 0.25; 0.10–0.64) reduced in B.
Per-protocol analysis; mature epidemic context.
- Nicaragua (Study 67, cluster RCT, 19 motels; 6463 couples over 24 days): For commercial sex (11 motels),
health-education material reduced condom use (OR 0.89; 95% CI 0.84–0.94); in-room condom availability increased use (OR
1.31; 1.09–1.75); handing condoms to couples also increased use (OR 1.32; 1.03–1.61). Larger effects for non-commercial
sex with in-room availability (OR 1.81; 1.14–2.81). Objective outcome via used condom retrieval; strongest strategy was
in-room condom availability.

Risk-of-bias and implementation notes:
- Randomization level varied (individual vs cluster/community). Cluster trials (Thailand, Uganda, Nicaragua) reduced
contamination but require appropriate analysis (not always detailed in abstracts).
- Self-reported behavior is common; several studies used biomarker-confirmed STIs (Madagascar, Thailand, China, Mexico,
Uganda).
- Follow-up durations varied (1 month to 12 months; one community trial duration unspecified here).
- Attrition reported in some (South Africa 80/93 at 1 month).
- Some trials show statistically significant biomarker outcomes (Madagascar aggregate STIs; China any STD; Mexico STIs
and HIV incidence density; Uganda some STIs), while others report behavior change without biomarker confirmation or with
non-significant differences.

Overall synthesis relative to the review objective:
- Behavioral counseling and skills-based interventions among sex workers can increase consistent condom use and, in
several trials, reduce STI outcomes; however, effects on HIV incidence at community level were not observed in the
Uganda trial.
- Structural access interventions (e.g., in-room condoms in motels) are effective at increasing condom use in settings
with sex work.
- Female condom options can maintain high protection levels even when male condom use decreases, though some trials did
not reach statistical significance.
- Contextual and empowerment-based approaches (South Africa, Armenia, India microenterprise) may reduce risk behaviors
and address structural determinants (economic vulnerability, violence, substance use)."""

additional_context = """### 3. Additional context (if relevant):
- Citation details (authors/years) were not provided in the abstracts supplied; thus, the 'citation' field uses study
titles. If full citations are needed, please provide full references or allow web retrieval.

- Uganda community trial (Study 26) is not specific to sex workers but informs broader behavioral/STI strategies;
included as supplied.
- Nicaragua motel trial (Study 67) includes both commercial and non-commercial sex; commercial sex results most relevant
to sex workers were highlighted."""

  # Prepare narrative sections
  short_version = """### 1. Task outcome (short version):
  Extracted PICO, settings, study design, follow-up, and quantitative outcomes from 11 included studies of behavioral
  interventions among sex workers/clients (and related high-risk settings) in LMICs. Key findings: counseling-enhanced
  condom promotion modestly reduced aggregate STIs and increased condom use in Madagascar (ORs ~0.7 and 1.4);
  providing the option of female condoms in Thailand reduced unprotected acts and STD incidence rates but not
  significantly; an adapted VCT in China improved consistent condom use (OR 2.23) and reduced STDs (OR 0.44); a brief
  intervention in Mexico reduced combined STI incidence density (P=0.034) and HIV incidence density (P<0.001);
  community-level interventions in Uganda did not reduce HIV-1 incidence but improved some STI outcomes and condom
  use; motel-based structural interventions in Nicaragua showed in-room condom availability increased use (ORs
  1.31–1.81), while educational materials were ineffective or harmful for commercial sex. Other RCTs (South Africa,
  Armenia, Zimbabwe, India) showed improvements in risk behaviors and feasibility, with limited biomarker data in
  some."""

  detailed_version = """### 2. Task outcome (extremely detailed version):
  - Madagascar (Study 2, RCT, n=1000 FSWs): Peer+clinic counseling vs peer-only increased reported condom use (overall
  OR 1.4; 95% CI 1.1–1.8) and reduced aggregate STI prevalence (OR 0.7; 95% CI 0.5–0.9); specific STIs had ORs 0.7–0.8
  with CIs crossing/null for some. 6-month follow-up; STI biomarkers and self-reports; minimal confounding after
  adjustment.
  - Thailand (Study 3, cluster RCT by establishment; 249 vs 255 FSWs): Option to use female condoms yielded high
  overall condom use (≈98%), reduced unprotected acts (5.9% vs 7.1%; P=0.16) and STD incidence rates (2.81 vs 3.69/100
  PY; P=0.18), but not statistically significant. Female condom use sustained; design minimized cross-over.
  - Madagascar (Study 6, RCT, n=901): Adding clinic-based counseling to peer education (male+female condom promotion)
  showed no significant differences in aggregated STI prevalence or reported protection. 12-month follow-up; prior
  intensive male condom promotion exposure.
  - China Guangxi (Study 7, quasi-experimental, n=400 FSWs): Adapted VCT increased consistent condom use (OR 2.23; 95%
  CI 1.26–3.96) and reduced any STD infection at follow-up (OR 0.44; 95% CI 0.24–0.80); large gains in knowledge
  (p<.0001). 6-month follow-up; lab-confirmed STDs.
  - Mexico (Study 8, RCT, n=924 FSWs): 30-min behavioral intervention reduced cumulative STI incidence (P=0.049);
  combined STI incidence density 13.8 vs 24.92/100 PY (P=0.034) and HIV incidence density 0 vs 2.01/100 PY (P<0.001);
  protected acts increased, unprotected acts decreased (P<0.05). 6-month follow-up; multiple biomarkers.
  - South Africa (Study 10, RCT, n=93; 80 at 1-mo): Woman-Focused intervention decreased unprotected sex and daily
  alcohol/cocaine use; greater substance-use reductions vs Standard; lower victimization reported. Short follow-up;
  self-reports; feasibility shown.
  - Armenia (Study 12, RCT, n=120 street-based FSWs): 2-hour, skills-based/gender-empowerment session increased
  consistent condom use (P=0.004) and performing condom application (P=0.0001) over 6 months; psychosocial mediators
  improved.
  - Zimbabwe (Study 14, RCT, n=149): Access to male+female vs male-only condoms increased consistent male condom use
  with clients by 2 weeks (0→52% vs 0→82%); female condom use remained low (3–9%); STI incidence 16/100 woman-months;
  lower use with boyfriends; high baseline HIV (86%) and 34% STI.
  - India, Chennai (Study 15, RCT pilot, n=100): Microenterprise (canvas bag tailoring) associated with fewer paying
  clients per month and increased income; fewer sex partners; sustained engagement in bag production; no biomarker
  data in abstract.
  - Uganda (Study 26, community cluster RCT, 18 communities): Behavioral (A) and behavioral+STI (B) vs control (C): No
  HIV-1 incidence reduction (A vs C RR 0.94; 95% CI 0.60–1.45; p=0.72; B vs C RR 1.00; 0.63–1.58; p=0.98). Condom use
  with last casual partner improved, significantly in B (PR 1.27; 1.02–1.56). HSV-2 incidence reduced in A (RR 0.65;
  0.53–0.80); active syphilis (RR 0.52; 0.27–0.98) and gonorrhoea prevalence (RR 0.25; 0.10–0.64) reduced in B.
  Per-protocol analysis; mature epidemic context.
  - Nicaragua (Study 67, cluster RCT, 19 motels; 6463 couples over 24 days): For commercial sex (11 motels),
  health-education material reduced condom use (OR 0.89; 95% CI 0.84–0.94); in-room condom availability increased use
  (OR 1.31; 1.09–1.75); handing condoms to couples also increased use (OR 1.32; 1.03–1.61). Larger effects for
  non-commercial sex with in-room availability (OR 1.81; 1.14–2.81). Objective outcome via used condom retrieval;
  strongest strategy was in-room condom availability.

  Risk-of-bias and implementation notes:
  - Randomization level varied (individual vs cluster/community). Cluster trials (Thailand, Uganda, Nicaragua) reduced
  contamination but require appropriate analysis (not always detailed in abstracts).
  - Self-reported behavior is common; several studies used biomarker-confirmed STIs (Madagascar, Thailand, China,
  Mexico, Uganda).
  - Follow-up durations varied (1 month to 12 months; one community trial duration unspecified here).
  - Attrition reported in some (South Africa 80/93 at 1 month).
  - Some trials show statistically significant biomarker outcomes (Madagascar aggregate STIs; China any STD; Mexico
  STIs and HIV incidence density; Uganda some STIs), while others report behavior change without biomarker
  confirmation or with non-significant differences.

  Overall synthesis relative to the review objective:
  - Behavioral counseling and skills-based interventions among sex workers can increase consistent condom use and, in
  several trials, reduce STI outcomes; however, effects on HIV incidence at community level were not observed in the
  Uganda trial.
  - Structural access interventions (e.g., in-room condoms in motels) are effective at increasing condom use in
  settings with sex work.
  - Female condom options can maintain high protection levels even when male condom use decreases, though some trials
  did not reach statistical significance.
  - Contextual and empowerment-based approaches (South Africa, Armenia, India microenterprise) may reduce risk
  behaviors and address structural determinants (economic vulnerability, violence, substance use)."""

  additional_context = """### 3. Additional context (if relevant):

=== BATCH EVIDENCE EXTRACTION ===
Research question: To evaluate the effectiveness of behavioral interventions to reduce the transmission of HIV infection
among sex workers and their clients in low‐ and middle‐income countries.
Studies to extract from: 11

INSTRUCTIONS: For each study, extract PICO elements and key findings.
Return a JSON list of extraction objects.

--- Study 2 ---
Title: Results of a randomised trial of male condom promotion among Madagascar sex workers
Abstract: OBJECTIVES To test the effect of supplementing peer promotion of male condom use with clinic based 
counselling, measured in terms of STI prevalence and reported male condom use. METHODS 1000 female sex workers in 
Madagascar were randomised to two study arms: peer education supplemented by individual risk reduction counselling by a 
clinician (peer + clinic) versus condom promotion by peer educators only (peer only). STI testing was conducted at 
baseline and 6 months. Behavioural interviews were administered at baseline, 2, 4, and 6 months. RESULTS At baseline, 
women in the peer only arm had prevalences of 16.0%, 23.6%, and 12.1% for chlamydia, gonorrhoea, and trichomoniasis 
respectively, with an aggregate prevalence of 38.2%. Baseline STI prevalences for the peer + clinic arm were slightly 
lower and 34.1% in aggregate. At 6 months, aggregate STI prevalence increased in the peer only arm to 41.4%, whereas the
aggregate prevalence diminished slightly to 32.1% in the peer + clinic arm. In logistic regression analyses, the 
estimated odds ratios (ORs) for chlamydia, gonorrhoea, trichomoniasis, and aggregate STI were 0.7 (95% confidence 
interval 0.4 to 1.0), 0.7 (0.5 to 1.0), 0.8 (0.6 to 1.2), and 0.7 (0.5 to 0.9) respectively, comparing the peer + clinic
arm with the peer only arm. The logistic regression OR for reported condom use with clients in the past 30 days 
increased from 1.1 at 2 months to 1.8 at 6 months, comparing the peer + clinic arm with the peer only arm, and was 1.4 
overall (1.1 to 1.8). Adjustment for baseline factors changed the regression results little. CONCLUSIONS The impact of 
male condom promotion on behaviour can be heightened through more concentrated counselling on risk reduction. 
Persistently high STI prevalence despite increases in reported condom use by sex workers supports the need for 
multidimensional control programmes.

--- Study 3 ---
Title: Protection against sexually transmitted diseases by granting sex workers in Thailand the choice from using the 
male or female condom: results from a randomized controlled trial
Abstract: BACKGROUND The male condom is the most effective barrier method available for protection against sexually 
transmitted diseases (STDs), including HIV infection. There is an urgent need to develop and evaluate other prevention 
methods, such as the female condom. This study estimated the additional protection against STDs offered to sex workers 
by giving them the option of using the female condom when clients refused to use a male condom. METHODS Sex 
establishments in four cities in Thailand were randomized into two study groups: one in which sex workers were 
instructed to use male condoms consistently (male condom group); and one in which sex workers had the option of using 
the female condom if clients refused or were not able to use male condoms (male/female condom group). Randomization was 
done by sex establishments, and not by individuals, to minimize sharing of female condoms across study groups. The 
proportion of unprotected sexual acts (defined as sexual acts in which condoms were not used, tore, or slipped in or 
out) and incidence rate of STDs (gonorrhoea, chlamydial infection, trichomoniasis and genital ulcer disease) were 
measured over a 24-week period and compared between the two study groups. FINDINGS Results are available from 34 sex 
establishments (249 women) in the male/female condom group, and 37 sex establishments (255 women) in the male condom 
group. Condom use was very high in both groups (97.9 and 97.3 % of all sexual acts, respectively, P > 0.05). Male condom
use was lower in the male/female condom group when compared with the male condom group (88.2 and 97.5%, respectively, P 
< 0.001). However, this reduction in male condom use was counterbalanced by the use of female condoms in 12.0% of all 
sexual acts in the male/female condom group, contributing to a 17% reduction in the proportion of unprotected sexual 
acts in this group when compared to the male condom group (5.9 versus 7.1%, respectively, P = 0.16). Female condom use 
was sustained over the entire study period. There was also a 24% reduction in the weighted geometric mean incidence rate
of STDs in the sex establishments of the male/female condom group compared to the male condom group (2.81 versus 3.69 
per 100 person-weeks, P = 0.18).

--- Study 6 ---
Title: Randomised controlled trial of alternative male and female condom promotion strategies targeting sex workers in 
Madagascar
Abstract: OBJECTIVES To assess whether individual clinic-based counselling as a supplement to peer education for male 
and female condom promotion leads to greater use of protection and lower STI prevalence among sex workers in Madagascar 
already exposed to intensive male condom promotion. METHODS In two public dispensaries in Madagascar, a total of 901 sex
workers were randomly allocated between two alternative male and female condom promotion INTERVENTIONS peer education 
only, or peer education supplemented with individual clinic-based counselling. Participants were followed for 12 months.
Every 2 months they made clinic visits, where they were interviewed on condom use. Peer educators counselled all 
participants on condom use as they accompanied their assigned participants to study visits. Participants assigned to 
receive the supplemental intervention were counselled by a trained clinician following study interviews. Participants 
were tested and treated for chlamydia, gonorrhoea and trichomoniasis every 6 months. We used logistic regression to 
assess whether the more intensive intervention was associated with reduced STI prevalence. Use of protection with 
clients and non-paying partners was assessed by study arm, site, and visit. RESULTS There was no statistically 
significant association between study arm and aggregated STI prevalence. No substantial differences in levels of 
reported protection were noted between study groups. CONCLUSIONS This study found little evidence for gains from more 
thorough clinical counselling on male and female condom use. These findings suggest that less clinically intensive 
interventions such as peer education could be suitable for male and female condom promotion in populations already 
exposed to barrier method promotion.

--- Study 7 ---
Title: Short‐term effect of a cultural adaptation of voluntary counseling and testing among female sex workers in China:
a quasi‐experimental trial
Abstract: This study evaluates the efficacy of cultural adaptation of a voluntary counseling and testing (VCT) 
intervention, in increasing condom use and decreasing rates of sexually transmitted diseases (STDs) among a group of 
female sex workers (FSWs) in Guangxi, China. This intervention is modeled after the "state-of-the-science" VCT program 
that was developed and evaluated by the Center for Disease Control and Prevention's Project RESPECT. Four hundred FSWs 
were assigned to either an intervention group receiving the VCT intervention or a control group receiving standard of 
care STD testing and treatment. Data were collected at baseline and 6 months postintervention. Outcome measures included
HIV/STD related knowledge and perceptions, condom use, and history of STDs. Five common STDs were screened and tested 
through clinical examination and laboratory testing to serve as biomarkers. After controlling for potential confounders 
and baseline differences, the VCT intervention group was significantly higher than the control group in HIV/STD related 
knowledge (p < .0001) and consistent condom use with clients (odds ration [OR] = 2.23; 95% confidence interval [CI] = 
1.26-3.96) at 6 months follow-up. In addition, the intervention group had a significantly lower infection rate of STDs 
than the control group at follow-up (OR = 0.44; 95% CI = 0.24-0.80). This quasi-experimental trial provides evidence 
that the brief VCT intervention, through appropriate cultural adaptation, can be efficacious in increasing condom use 
and reducing STD infection rate among FSWs in China.

--- Study 8 ---
Title: Efficacy of a brief behavioral intervention to promote condom use among female se workers in Tijuana and Ciudad 
Juarez, Mexico
Abstract: OBJECTIVES We examined the efficacy of a brief behavioral intervention to promote condom use among female sex 
workers in Tijuana and Ciudad Juarez, Mexico. METHODS We randomized 924 female sex workers 18 years or older without 
known HIV infection living in Tijuana and Ciudad Juarez who had recently had unprotected sex with clients to a 30-minute
behavioral intervention or a didactic control condition. At baseline and 6 months, women underwent interviews and 
testing for HIV, syphilis, gonorrhea, and chlamydia. RESULTS We observed a 40% decline in cumulative sexually 
transmitted illness incidence (P = .049) in the intervention group. Incidence density for the intervention versus 
control groups was 13.8 versus 24.92 per 100 person-years for sexually transmitted illnesses combined (P = .034) and 0 
versus 2.01 per 100 person-years for HIV (P < .001). There were concomitant increases in the number and percentage of 
protected sex acts and decreases in the number of unprotected sex acts with clients (P < .05). CONCLUSIONS This brief 
behavioral intervention shows promise in reducing HIV and sexually transmitted illness risk behaviors among female sex 
workers and may be transferable to other resource-constrained settings.

--- Study 10 ---
Title: Substance use, sexual risk, and violence: HIV prevention intervention with sex workers in Pretoria
Abstract: This paper describes an HIV prevention intervention designed in the US that was adapted and implemented in 
South Africa. Using an experimental design, 93 women who reported recent substance use and sex trading were randomly 
assigned to a modified Standard HIV intervention or to a Woman-Focused HIV prevention intervention. Eighty women 
completed the one-month follow-up interview. Participants reported high rates of sexual risk and violence at baseline. 
At follow-up, findings showed decreases in the proportion of women reporting unprotected sex and the daily use of 
alcohol and cocaine. Daily alcohol and cocaine use decreased more for women receiving the Woman-Focused intervention. 
Although violence continued to be a problem, at follow-up Woman-Focused participants reported being victimized less 
often than women receiving the Standard intervention. This study demonstrates the feasibility of implementing 
cross-cultural behavioral HIV prevention interventions, and supports the need for future studies of women's contextual 
issues and the effectiveness of targeted interventions.

--- Study 12 ---
Title: A randomized controlled trial of an HIV prevention intervention for street‐based female sex workers in Yerevan, 
Armenia: preliminary evidence of efficacy
Abstract: This study evaluated the efficacy of an HIV intervention among female sex workers (FSWs) randomized to an 
intervention or wait-list control. FSWs (N = 120) completed baseline, 3- and 6-month assessments. A health educator 
implemented 2-hour intervention emphasized gender-empowerment, self-efficacy to persuade clients to use condoms, condom 
application skills, and eroticizing safer sex. Over the 6-month follow-up, FSWs in the intervention reported more 
consistent condom use with clients (P = .004) and were more likely to apply condoms on clients (P = .0001). Intervention
effects were observed for other psychosocial mediators of safer sex. Brief, gender and culturally congruent 
interventions can enhance HIV-preventive behaviors among FSWs.Springer

--- Study 14 ---
Title: Constraints faced by sex workers in use of female and male condoms for safer sex in urban Zimbabwe
Abstract: We investigated whether female condoms are acceptable to sex workers in Harare and whether improved access to 
male and female condoms increases the proportion of protected sex episodes with clients and boyfriends. Sex workers were
randomly placed in groups to receive either male and female condoms (group A, n=99) or male condoms only (group B, n=50)
and were followed prospectively for about 3 months each. We found a considerable burden of human immunodeficiency virus 
(HIV) and sexually transmitted infections (STIs) in our cohort at enrollment (86% tested HIV positive and 34% had at 
least one STI). Consistent male condom use with clients increased from 0% to 52% in group A and from 0% to 82% in group 
B between enrollment and first follow-up 2 weeks later and remained high throughout the study. Few women in group A 
reported using female condoms with clients consistently (3%–9%), and use of either condom was less common with 
boyfriends than with clients throughout the study (8%–39%) for different study groups, visits, and types of condom). 
Unprotected sex still took place, as evidenced by an STI incidence of 16 episodes per 100 woman-months of follow-up. Our
questionnaire data indicated high self-reported acceptability of female condoms, but focus group discussions revealed 
that a main obstacle to female condom use was client distrust of unfamiliar methods. This study shows that a simple 
intervention of improving access to condoms can lead to more protected sex episodes between sex workers and clients. 
However, more work is needed to help sex workers achieve safer sex in noncommercial relationships.Springer

--- Study 15 ---
Title: Acceptability of a microenterprise intervention among female sex workers in Chennai, India
Abstract: Female sex workers have been central in India’s HIV epidemic since it was first diagnosed among them in 1989. 
Female sex workers’ risk of HIV is primarily economically motivated. The Pi pilot study examined the feasibility and 
association of a microenterprise intervention, the tailoring of canvas bags, on sexual risk behaviors among female sex 
workers (N = 100) in Chennai. Women were randomized to an intervention or control arm. Between-group comparisons at 
baseline and at six-month follow-up were performed. Multivariate linear regression with bootstrapping was conducted to 
estimate the intervention effect. At baseline, women were a median of 35 years old, 61% were married and they had an 
average of two children. Intervention participants reported a significantly lower number of sex partners and significant
increases in income at the 6-month follow-up compared to control participants. In a multivariate model, intervention 
participants had a significantly lower number of paying clients per month at follow-up compared to control participants.
By graduation, 75% of intervention arm participants had made at least one sellable canvas bag and 6 months after the 
study’s end, 60% have continued involvement in bag production. The pilot study demonstrated that microenterprise 
interventions are successful in both providing FSWs with licit income opportunities and was associated with reductions 
in HIV risk behaviors.Springer

--- Study 26 ---
Title: Syndromic management of sexually‐transmitted infections and behavior change interventions on transmission of 
HIV‐1 in rural Uganda: a community randomised trial
Abstract: BACKGROUND Treatment of sexually-transmitted infections (STIs) and behavioural interventions are the main 
methods to prevent HIV in developing countries. We aimed to assess the effect of these interventions on incidence of 
HIV-1 and other sexually-transmitted infections. METHODS We randomly allocated all adults living in 18 communities in 
rural Uganda to receive behavioural interventions alone (group A), behavioural and STI interventions (group B), or 
routine government health services and community development activities (group C). The primary outcome was HIV-1 
incidence. Secondary outcomes were incidence of herpes simplex virus type 2 (HSV2) and active syphilis and prevalence of
gonorrhoea, chlamydia, reported genital ulcers, reported genital discharge, and markers of behavioural change. Analysis 
was per protocol. FINDINGS Compared with group C, the incidence rate ratio of HIV-1 was 0.94 (0.60-1.45, p=0.72) in 
group A and 1.00 (0.63-1.58, p=0.98) in group B, and the prevalence ratio of use of condoms with last casual partner was
1.12 (95% CI 0.99-1.25) in group A and 1.27 (1.02-1.56) in group B. Incidence of HSV2 was lower in group A than in group
C (incidence rate ratio 0.65, 0.53-0.80) and incidence of active syphilis for high rapid plasma reagent test titre and 
prevalence of gonorrhoea were both lower in group B than in group C (active syphilis incidence rate ratio, 0.52, 
0.27-0.98; gonorrhoea prevalence ratio, 0.25, 0.10-0.64). INTERPRETATION The interventions we used were insufficient to 
reduce HIV-1 incidence in rural Uganda, where secular changes are occurring. More effective STI and behavioural 
interventions need to be developed for HIV control in mature epidemics.

--- Study 67 ---
Title: Promotion of condom use in a high‐risk setting in Nicaragua: a randomised controlled trial
Abstract: BackgroundIn Latin America, motels rent rooms for commercial and non-commercial sex. We investigated the 
impact of providing health-education material and condoms on condom use in Managua, Nicaragua.MethodsIn a randomised 
controlled trial, in 19 motels, we gave condoms on request, made them available in rooms, or gave condoms directly to 
couples, with and without the presence of health-education material in the rooms. In a factorial design we assessed 
condom use directly by searching the rooms after couples had left.Findings11 motels were used mainly by sex workers and 
their clients and eight mainly for non-commercial sex. 6463 couples attended the motels in 24 days. On 3106 (48·0%) 
occasions, at least one used condom was retrieved. Condom use was more frequent for commercial sex than for 
non-commercial sex (60·5 vs 20·2%). The presence of health-education material lowered the frequency of condom use for 
commercial sex (odds ratio 0·89 [95% CI 0·84–0·94]) and had no effect on use for non-commercial sex (1·03 [0·97–1·08]). 
Condom use increased for commercial (1·31 [1·09–1·75]) and noncommercial sex (1·81 (1·14–2·81) if condoms were available
in rooms. Directly handing condoms to couples was similarly effective for commercial sex but less effective for 
non-commercial sex (1·32 [1·03–1·61] vs 1·52 [1·01–2·38]).InterpretationIn Latin America, motels are key locations for 
promoting the use of condoms. Making condoms available in rooms is the most effective strategy to increase condom use, 
whereas use of health-education material was ineffective. These findings have important implications for HIV-prevention 
policies.thelancet.com

### 1. Task outcome (short version):
Extracted PICO, settings, study design, follow-up, and quantitative outcomes from 11 included studies of behavioral 
interventions among sex workers/clients (and related high-risk settings) in LMICs. Key findings: counseling-enhanced 
condom promotion modestly reduced aggregate STIs and increased condom use in Madagascar (ORs ~0.7 and 1.4); providing 
the option of female condoms in Thailand reduced unprotected acts and STD incidence rates but not significantly; an 
adapted VCT in China improved consistent condom use (OR 2.23) and reduced STDs (OR 0.44); a brief intervention in Mexico
reduced combined STI incidence density (P=0.034) and HIV incidence density (P<0.001); community-level interventions in 
Uganda did not reduce HIV-1 incidence but improved some STI outcomes and condom use; motel-based structural 
interventions in Nicaragua showed in-room condom availability increased use (ORs 1.31–1.81), while educational materials
were ineffective or harmful for commercial sex. Other RCTs (South Africa, Armenia, Zimbabwe, India) showed improvements 
in risk behaviors and feasibility, with limited biomarker data in some.

### 2. Task outcome (extremely detailed version):
- Madagascar (Study 2, RCT, n=1000 FSWs): Peer+clinic counseling vs peer-only increased reported condom use (overall OR 
1.4; 95% CI 1.1–1.8) and reduced aggregate STI prevalence (OR 0.7; 95% CI 0.5–0.9); specific STIs had ORs 0.7–0.8 with 
CIs crossing/null for some. 6-month follow-up; STI biomarkers and self-reports; minimal confounding after adjustment.
- Thailand (Study 3, cluster RCT by establishment; 249 vs 255 FSWs): Option to use female condoms yielded high overall 
condom use (≈98%), reduced unprotected acts (5.9% vs 7.1%; P=0.16) and STD incidence rates (2.81 vs 3.69/100 PY; 
P=0.18), but not statistically significant. Female condom use sustained; design minimized cross-over.
- Madagascar (Study 6, RCT, n=901): Adding clinic-based counseling to peer education (male+female condom promotion) 
showed no significant differences in aggregated STI prevalence or reported protection. 12-month follow-up; prior 
intensive male condom promotion exposure.
- China Guangxi (Study 7, quasi-experimental, n=400 FSWs): Adapted VCT increased consistent condom use (OR 2.23; 95% CI 
1.26–3.96) and reduced any STD infection at follow-up (OR 0.44; 95% CI 0.24–0.80); large gains in knowledge (p<.0001). 
6-month follow-up; lab-confirmed STDs.
- Mexico (Study 8, RCT, n=924 FSWs): 30-min behavioral intervention reduced cumulative STI incidence (P=0.049); combined
STI incidence density 13.8 vs 24.92/100 PY (P=0.034) and HIV incidence density 0 vs 2.01/100 PY (P<0.001); protected 
acts increased, unprotected acts decreased (P<0.05). 6-month follow-up; multiple biomarkers.
- South Africa (Study 10, RCT, n=93; 80 at 1-mo): Woman-Focused intervention decreased unprotected sex and daily 
alcohol/cocaine use; greater substance-use reductions vs Standard; lower victimization reported. Short follow-up; 
self-reports; feasibility shown.
- Armenia (Study 12, RCT, n=120 street-based FSWs): 2-hour, skills-based/gender-empowerment session increased consistent
condom use (P=0.004) and performing condom application (P=0.0001) over 6 months; psychosocial mediators improved.
- Zimbabwe (Study 14, RCT, n=149): Access to male+female vs male-only condoms increased consistent male condom use with 
clients by 2 weeks (0→52% vs 0→82%); female condom use remained low (3–9%); STI incidence 16/100 woman-months; lower use
with boyfriends; high baseline HIV (86%) and 34% STI.
- India, Chennai (Study 15, RCT pilot, n=100): Microenterprise (canvas bag tailoring) associated with fewer paying 
clients per month and increased income; fewer sex partners; sustained engagement in bag production; no biomarker data in
abstract.
- Uganda (Study 26, community cluster RCT, 18 communities): Behavioral (A) and behavioral+STI (B) vs control (C): No 
HIV-1 incidence reduction (A vs C RR 0.94; 95% CI 0.60–1.45; p=0.72; B vs C RR 1.00; 0.63–1.58; p=0.98). Condom use with
last casual partner improved, significantly in B (PR 1.27; 1.02–1.56). HSV-2 incidence reduced in A (RR 0.65; 
0.53–0.80); active syphilis (RR 0.52; 0.27–0.98) and gonorrhoea prevalence (RR 0.25; 0.10–0.64) reduced in B. 
Per-protocol analysis; mature epidemic context.
- Nicaragua (Study 67, cluster RCT, 19 motels; 6463 couples over 24 days): For commercial sex (11 motels), 
health-education material reduced condom use (OR 0.89; 95% CI 0.84–0.94); in-room condom availability increased use (OR 
1.31; 1.09–1.75); handing condoms to couples also increased use (OR 1.32; 1.03–1.61). Larger effects for non-commercial 
sex with in-room availability (OR 1.81; 1.14–2.81). Objective outcome via used condom retrieval; strongest strategy was 
in-room condom availability.

Risk-of-bias and implementation notes:
- Randomization level varied (individual vs cluster/community). Cluster trials (Thailand, Uganda, Nicaragua) reduced 
contamination but require appropriate analysis (not always detailed in abstracts).
- Self-reported behavior is common; several studies used biomarker-confirmed STIs (Madagascar, Thailand, China, Mexico, 
Uganda).
- Follow-up durations varied (1 month to 12 months; one community trial duration unspecified here).
- Attrition reported in some (South Africa 80/93 at 1 month).
- Some trials show statistically significant biomarker outcomes (Madagascar aggregate STIs; China any STD; Mexico STIs 
and HIV incidence density; Uganda some STIs), while others report behavior change without biomarker confirmation or with
non-significant differences.

Overall synthesis relative to the review objective:
- Behavioral counseling and skills-based interventions among sex workers can increase consistent condom use and, in 
several trials, reduce STI outcomes; however, effects on HIV incidence at community level were not observed in the 
Uganda trial.
- Structural access interventions (e.g., in-room condoms in motels) are effective at increasing condom use in settings 
with sex work.
- Female condom options can maintain high protection levels even when male condom use decreases, though some trials did 
not reach statistical significance.
- Contextual and empowerment-based approaches (South Africa, Armenia, India microenterprise) may reduce risk behaviors 
and address structural determinants (economic vulnerability, violence, substance use).

### 3. Additional context (if relevant):
- Citation details (authors/years) were not provided in the abstracts supplied; thus, the 'citation' field uses study 
titles. If full citations are needed, please provide full references or allow web retrieval.
- Where only p-value thresholds were given (e.g., P<0.001), exact p-values were not imputed; they are narrated in key 
findings.
- For outcomes without explicitly reported effect measures/sizes, fields are set to null and detailed quantitatively 
(e.g., raw rates) in outcome names/key findings.
- Uganda community trial (Study 26) is not specific to sex workers but informs broader behavioral/STI strategies; 
included as supplied.
- Nicaragua motel trial (Study 67) includes both commercial and non-commercial sex; commercial sex results most relevant
to sex workers were highlighted.

version):\nExtracted PICO, settings, study design, follow-up, and quantitative outcomes from 11 included studies of
behavioral interventions among sex workers/clients (and related high-risk settings) in LMICs. Key findings:
counseling-enhanced condom promotion modestly reduced aggregate STIs and increased condom use in Madagascar (ORs
~0.7 and 1.4); providing the option of female condoms in Thailand reduced unprotected acts and STD incidence rates
but not significantly; an adapted VCT in China improved consistent condom use (OR 2.23) and reduced STDs (OR 0.44);
a brief intervention in Mexico reduced combined STI incidence density (P=0.034) and HIV incidence density (P<0.001);
community-level interventions in Uganda did not reduce HIV-1 incidence but improved some STI outcomes and condom
use; motel-based structural interventions in Nicaragua showed in-room condom availability increased use (ORs
1.31–1.81), while educational materials were ineffective or harmful for commercial sex. Other RCTs (South Africa,
Armenia, Zimbabwe, India) showed improvements in risk behaviors and feasibility, with limited biomarker data in
some.\n\n### 2. Task outcome (extremely detailed version):\n- Madagascar (Study 2, RCT, n=1000 FSWs): Peer+clinic
counseling vs peer-only increased reported condom use (overall OR 1.4; 95% CI 1.1–1.8) and reduced aggregate STI
prevalence (OR 0.7; 95% CI 0.5–0.9); specific STIs had ORs 0.7–0.8 with CIs crossing/null for some. 6-month
follow-up; STI biomarkers and self-reports; minimal confounding after adjustment.\n- Thailand (Study 3, cluster RCT
by establishment; 249 vs 255 FSWs): Option to use female condoms yielded high overall condom use (≈98%), reduced
unprotected acts (5.9% vs 7.1%; P=0.16) and STD incidence rates (2.81 vs 3.69/100 PY; P=0.18), but not statistically
significant. Female condom use sustained; design minimized cross-over.\n- Madagascar (Study 6, RCT, n=901): Adding
clinic-based counseling to peer education (male+female condom promotion) showed no significant differences in
aggregated STI prevalence or reported protection. 12-month follow-up; prior intensive male condom promotion
exposure.\n- China Guangxi (Study 7, quasi-experimental, n=400 FSWs): Adapted VCT increased consistent condom use
(OR 2.23; 95% CI 1.26–3.96) and reduced any STD infection at follow-up (OR 0.44; 95% CI 0.24–0.80); large gains in
knowledge (p<.0001). 6-month follow-up; lab-confirmed STDs.\n- Mexico (Study 8, RCT, n=924 FSWs): 30-min behavioral
intervention reduced cumulative STI incidence (P=0.049); combined STI incidence density 13.8 vs 24.92/100 PY
(P=0.034) and HIV incidence density 0 vs 2.01/100 PY (P<0.001); protected acts increased, unprotected acts decreased
(P<0.05). 6-month follow-up; multiple biomarkers.\n- South Africa (Study 10, RCT, n=93; 80 at 1-mo): Woman-Focused
intervention decreased unprotected sex and daily alcohol/cocaine use; greater substance-use reductions vs Standard;
lower victimization reported. Short follow-up; self-reports; feasibility shown.\n- Armenia (Study 12, RCT, n=120
street-based FSWs): 2-hour, skills-based/gender-empowerment session increased consistent condom use (P=0.004) and
performing condom application (P=0.0001) over 6 months; psychosocial mediators improved.\n- Zimbabwe (Study 14, RCT,
n=149): Access to male+female vs male-only condoms increased consistent male condom use with clients by 2 weeks
(0→52% vs 0→82%); female condom use remained low (3–9%); STI incidence 16/100 woman-months; lower use with
boyfriends; high baseline HIV (86%) and 34% STI.\n- India, Chennai (Study 15, RCT pilot, n=100): Microenterprise
(canvas bag tailoring) associated with fewer paying clients per month and increased income; fewer sex partners;
sustained engagement in bag production; no biomarker data in abstract.\n- Uganda (Study 26, community cluster RCT,
18 communities): Behavioral (A) and behavioral+STI (B) vs control (C): No HIV-1 incidence reduction (A vs C RR 0.94;
95% CI 0.60–1.45; p=0.72; B vs C RR 1.00; 0.63–1.58; p=0.98). Condom use with last casual partner improved,
significantly in B (PR 1.27; 1.02–1.56). HSV-2 incidence reduced in A (RR 0.65; 0.53–0.80); active syphilis (RR
0.52; 0.27–0.98) and gonorrhoea prevalence (RR 0.25; 0.10–0.64) reduced in B. Per-protocol analysis; mature epidemic
context.\n- Nicaragua (Study 67, cluster RCT, 19 motels; 6463 couples over 24 days): For commercial sex (11 motels),
health-education material reduced condom use (OR 0.89; 95% CI 0.84–0.94); in-room condom availability increased use
(OR 1.31; 1.09–1.75); handing condoms to couples also increased use (OR 1.32; 1.03–1.61). Larger effects for
non-commercial sex with in-room availability (OR 1.81; 1.14–2.81). Objective outcome via used condom retrieval;
strongest strategy was in-room condom availability.\n\nRisk-of-bias and implementation notes:\n- Randomization level
varied (individual vs cluster/community). Cluster trials (Thailand, Uganda, Nicaragua) reduced contamination but
require appropriate analysis (not always detailed in abstracts).\n- Self-reported behavior is common; several
studies used biomarker-confirmed STIs (Madagascar, Thailand, China, Mexico, Uganda).\n- Follow-up durations varied
(1 month to 12 months; one community trial duration unspecified here).\n- Attrition reported in some (South Africa
80/93 at 1 month).\n- Some trials show statistically significant biomarker outcomes (Madagascar aggregate STIs;
China any STD; Mexico STIs and HIV incidence density; Uganda some STIs), while others report behavior change without
biomarker confirmation or with non-significant differences.\n\nOverall synthesis relative to the review
objective:\n- Behavioral counseling and skills-based interventions among sex workers can increase consistent condom
use and, in several trials, reduce STI outcomes; however, effects on HIV incidence at community level were not
observed in the Uganda trial.\n- Structural access interventions (e.g., in-room condoms in motels) are effective at
increasing condom use in settings with sex work.\n- Female condom options can maintain high protection levels even
when male condom use decreases, though some trials did not reach statistical significance.\n- Contextual and
empowerment-based approaches (South Africa, Armenia, India microenterprise) may reduce risk behaviors and address
structural determinants (economic vulnerability, violence, substance use).\n\n### 3. Additional context (if
relevant):\n- Citation details (authors/years) were not provided in the abstracts supplied; thus, the \'citation\'
field uses study titles. If full citations are needed, please provide full references or allow web retrieval.\n-
Where only p-value thresholds were given (e.g., P<0.001), exact p-values were not imputed; they are narrated in key
findings.\n- For outcomes without explicitly reported effect measures/sizes, fields are set to null and detailed
quantitatively (e.g., raw rates) in outcome names/key findings.\n- Uganda community trial (Study 26) is not specific
to sex workers but informs broader behavioral/STI strategies; included as supplied.\n- Nicaragua motel trial (Study
67) includes both commercial and non-commercial sex; commercial sex results most relevant to sex workers were
highlighted.', 'review_objective': 'To evaluate the effectiveness of behavioral interventions to reduce the
transmission of HIV infection among sex workers and their clients in low‐ and middle‐income countries.'}.

import json
import re

# The variables `evidence_json` and `review_objective` are provided by the system.

def extract_studies_block(evidence_text):
    # Find the JSON object that starts with {"studies": [...]}
    start_idx = evidence_text.find('{"studies"')
    if start_idx == -1:
        return None
    s = evidence_text[start_idx:]
    depth = 0
    end_idx = None
    for i, ch in enumerate(s):
        if ch == '{':
            depth += 1
        elif ch == '}':
            depth -= 1
            if depth == 0:
                end_idx = i + 1
                break
    if end_idx is None:
        return None
    return s[:end_idx]

studies_json_str = extract_studies_block(evidence_json)
parsed = None
if studies_json_str:
    try:
        parsed = json.loads(studies_json_str)
    except Exception as e:
        parsed = None

if parsed is None or "studies" not in parsed:
    print("ERROR: Could not parse extracted studies JSON.")
else:
    study_indices = [s.get("study_index") for s in parsed["studies"]]
    print(f"Parsed {len(parsed['studies'])} studies. Indices: {study_indices}")

# Keep a clean JSON string for tool calls
extracted_json_str = json.dumps(parsed) if parsed is not None else None
print("Prepared extracted_json_str for tool calls:", "yes" if extracted_json_str else "no")

    "0.27–0.98; combined arm), and gonorrhoea prevalence (RR 0.25; 0.10–0.64; combined arm). By contrast, a 12-month RCT "
    "in Madagascar [6] found no significant differences in aggregated STI prevalence, potentially reflecting high prior "
    "condom promotion and contextual factors. In Thailand [3], STD incidence rates were 24% lower with the option of "
    "female condoms but not statistically significant (2.81 vs 3.69 per 100 person-weeks; P=0.18). Overall, evidence "
    "supports that targeted behavioral/skills-based counseling and select structural elements can reduce non-HIV STI "
    "burden among sex workers, though effects may vary by context, baseline prevention saturation, and power.\n\n"
    "Condom use: Several trials showed improvements in protected sex. Madagascar [2] reported higher overall condom use "
    "with clients in the peer+clinic arm (OR 1.4; 95% CI 1.1–1.8), with effects strengthening across follow-up. In China [7], "
    "consistent condom use with clients increased (OR 2.23; 95% CI 1.26–3.96). Armenia [12] found higher consistent condom "
    "use over 6 months (P=0.004) and improved application skills. In Zimbabwe [14], access to male and female condoms increased "
    "protected sex with clients in both groups; male condom consistency rose more in the male-only group (0%→82% vs 0%→52% "
    "by 2 weeks), while the male+female group showed modest female condom uptake (3%–9%). In Thailand [3], permitting female "
    "condoms yielded fewer unprotected acts (5.9% vs 7.1%; P=0.16), though effects were not significant. A large motel-based "
    "structural cRCT in Nicaragua [67] showed that in-room condom availability increased condom use for commercial sex (OR 1.31; "
    "95% CI 1.09–1.75) and non-commercial sex (OR 1.81; 1.14–2.81), whereas health-education materials alone were ineffective "
    "or even reduced use for commercial sex (OR 0.89; 0.84–0.94). Mexico [8] documented increases in protected acts and declines "
    "in unprotected acts (P<0.05). South Africa [10] reported reductions in unprotected sex at 1 month. Collectively, "
    "skills-based counseling and structural access (especially convenient condom availability) reliably increase protected "
    "sex, though magnitudes vary and ceiling effects can attenuate differences.\n\n"
    "Other HIV-related outcomes: Interventions often improved proximal determinants of risk. Knowledge gains were marked in "
    "China [7] (p<0.0001). The Woman-Focused program in South Africa [10] reduced daily alcohol/cocaine use and reported "
    "victimization at 1 month, addressing key co-factors of HIV risk. A microenterprise pilot in India [15] reduced the number "
    "of paying clients and increased income, suggesting potential to lower exposure by addressing economic vulnerability. "

    "Zimbabwe [14], Uganda [26]), Asia (Thailand [3], China [7], Armenia [12], India [15]), and Latin America (Mexico [8], Nicaragua [67]). "
    "Populations varied (street-based vs establishment-based FSWs; motel-based commercial sex), baseline prevention exposure, and epidemic "
    "context. Outcomes mixed objective biomarkers and self-reports, with follow-up ranging from 24 days to 12 months.\n\n"
    "Overall interpretation: There is consistent evidence that behavioral counseling and structural condom access increase condom use "
    "among sex workers and clients, and multiple trials demonstrate reductions in non-HIV STIs. Evidence for reducing HIV incidence "
    "is limited and context-specific, with one positive RCT signal in a short-term trial [8] and null effects at community scale [26]. "

### 1. Task outcome (short version):
Behavioral and structural interventions among sex workers/clients in LMICs consistently increase condom use and, in 
several trials, reduce non-HIV STIs. Evidence for HIV incidence reduction is limited: one RCT [8] showed lower HIV 
incidence density, while a large community cRCT found no effect [26]. Structural access (in-room condoms) robustly 
increases use [67]. Overall evidence strength: moderate; key gaps include sparse HIV incidence endpoints, short 
follow-up, heterogeneity, and reliance on self-report.

### 2. Task outcome (extremely detailed version):
HIV incidence/prevalence: Across studies involving sex workers and high-risk settings, evidence for reducing HIV 
incidence is limited. In Mexico [8], a brief behavioral intervention reduced HIV incidence density over ~6 months (0 vs 
2.01 per 100 person-years), alongside significant declines in combined STI incidence density. However, a large community
cluster trial in Uganda [26] observed no reduction in HIV-1 incidence with behavioral interventions alone (RR 0.94; 95% 
CI 0.60–1.45) or combined with STI services (RR 1.00; 0.63–1.58). No trials reported HIV prevalence reductions among sex
workers over longer horizons. Overall, HIV incidence findings remain sparse and context-dependent.

STI outcomes: Multiple studies reported biomarker-confirmed STI improvements. In Madagascar [2], adding clinic-based 
counseling to peer education reduced aggregate STI prevalence (OR 0.7; 95% CI 0.5–0.9), with consistent directions for 
chlamydia and gonorrhoea (ORs ~0.7). In China [7], culturally adapted VCT reduced any STD at follow-up (OR 0.44; 95% CI 
0.24–0.80). In Mexico [8], cumulative STI incidence declined (P=0.049) and combined STI incidence density fell to 13.8 
vs 24.92 per 100 person-years (P=0.034). In Uganda [26], although HIV incidence was unchanged, favorable effects were 
observed for HSV-2 incidence (RR 0.65; 0.53–0.80; behavioral arm), active syphilis incidence (RR 0.52; 0.27–0.98; 
combined arm), and gonorrhoea prevalence (RR 0.25; 0.10–0.64; combined arm). By contrast, a 12-month RCT in Madagascar 
[6] found no significant differences in aggregated STI prevalence, potentially reflecting high prior condom promotion 
and contextual factors. In Thailand [3], STD incidence rates were 24% lower with the option of female condoms but not 
statistically significant (2.81 vs 3.69 per 100 person-weeks; P=0.18). Overall, evidence supports that targeted 
behavioral/skills-based counseling and select structural elements can reduce non-HIV STI burden among sex workers, 
though effects may vary by context, baseline prevention saturation, and power.

Condom use: Several trials showed improvements in protected sex. Madagascar [2] reported higher overall condom use with 
clients in the peer+clinic arm (OR 1.4; 95% CI 1.1–1.8), with effects strengthening across follow-up. In China [7], 
consistent condom use with clients increased (OR 2.23; 95% CI 1.26–3.96). Armenia [12] found higher consistent condom 
use over 6 months (P=0.004) and improved application skills. In Zimbabwe [14], access to male and female condoms 
increased protected sex with clients in both groups; male condom consistency rose more in the male-only group (0%→82% vs
0%→52% by 2 weeks), while the male+female group showed modest female condom uptake (3%–9%). In Thailand [3], permitting 
female condoms yielded fewer unprotected acts (5.9% vs 7.1%; P=0.16), though effects were not significant. A large 
motel-based structural cRCT in Nicaragua [67] showed that in-room condom availability increased condom use for 
commercial sex (OR 1.31; 95% CI 1.09–1.75) and non-commercial sex (OR 1.81; 1.14–2.81), whereas health-education 
materials alone were ineffective or even reduced use for commercial sex (OR 0.89; 0.84–0.94). Mexico [8] documented 
increases in protected acts and declines in unprotected acts (P<0.05). South Africa [10] reported reductions in 
unprotected sex at 1 month. Collectively, skills-based counseling and structural access (especially convenient condom 
availability) reliably increase protected sex, though magnitudes vary and ceiling effects can attenuate differences.

Other HIV-related outcomes: Interventions often improved proximal determinants of risk. Knowledge gains were marked in 
China [7] (p<0.0001). The Woman-Focused program in South Africa [10] reduced daily alcohol/cocaine use and reported 
victimization at 1 month, addressing key co-factors of HIV risk. A microenterprise pilot in India [15] reduced the 
number of paying clients and increased income, suggesting potential to lower exposure by addressing economic 
vulnerability. These upstream changes are promising but are supported by smaller studies, short follow-up, and 
predominantly self-reported measures.

Heterogeneity: Interventions spanned individual-level counseling (peer+clinic risk-reduction [2], adapted VCT [7], brief
behavioral sessions [8,12]), device-choice strategies (adding female condoms [3,14]), structural access (in-room condoms
[67]), community-wide packages [26], and economic empowerment [15]. Settings covered Africa (Madagascar [2,6], South 
Africa [10], Zimbabwe [14], Uganda [26]), Asia (Thailand [3], China [7], Armenia [12], India [15]), and Latin America 
(Mexico [8], Nicaragua [67]). Populations varied (street-based vs establishment-based FSWs; motel-based commercial sex),
baseline prevention exposure, and epidemic context. Outcomes mixed objective biomarkers and self-reports, with follow-up
ranging from 24 days to 12 months.

Overall interpretation: There is consistent evidence that behavioral counseling and structural condom access increase 
condom use among sex workers and clients, and multiple trials demonstrate reductions in non-HIV STIs. Evidence for 
reducing HIV incidence is limited and context-specific, with one positive RCT signal in a short-term trial [8] and null 
effects at community scale [26]. Multi-component strategies that combine skills-based counseling, sustained and 
convenient condom availability, and structural supports (e.g., addressing substance use, violence, economic 
vulnerability) appear most promising for risk reduction and may be needed to achieve durable impacts on HIV 
transmission.

Conclusions and implications: Programs should pair skills-based counseling with reliable, convenient condom access, and 
integrate supports addressing substance use, violence, and economic vulnerability. Future research should prioritize 
adequately powered cluster-randomized or individually randomized trials with longer follow-up, HIV incidence endpoints, 
rigorous handling of clustering and attrition, and biomarker-validated outcomes. Implementation studies should assess 
scalability, sustained adoption (including female condom options), and effects among clients and regular partners.

### 3. Additional context (if relevant):
Study identifiers used for citation are those provided in the evidence JSON (e.g., [2], [3], [8]). Some abstracts lacked
details on analytic methods, clustering adjustments, or full effect sizes; appraisals reflect available information.

# Systematic Review Report

## 1. Review Summary
- **Title:** Behavioral interventions to reduce the transmission of HIV infection among sex workers and their clients in
low‐ and middle‐income countries
- **Objective:** To evaluate the effectiveness of behavioral interventions to reduce the transmission of HIV infection 
among sex workers and their clients in low‐ and middle‐income countries.

## 2. Search Results
- Number of candidate studies found: 85

  - Study 2: INCLUDE — Randomized controlled trial among sex workers comparing peer education plus clinic-based 
counseling vs peer-only; behavioral intervention with STI prevalence and self-reported condom use outcomes.
  - Study 3: INCLUDE — Cluster-randomized trial (establishment-level) offering option of female condom vs male condom 
only; behavioral prevention with outcomes on unprotected sex and STD incidence.

intervention with condom use and STI outcomes. Randomization unclear—include conservatively and flag uncertainty.
